summary.text: Writing \(m=n^2-2\) and \(q=m/\gcd(m,D)\), the identity \(2D=2(n-1)(n-3)!+m\sum_{j<n-3}j!\), together with Legendre’s factorial-valuation bound, shows that \(p^j\mid q\) forces \(p^{\lfloor(n-3)/p\rfloor+j}\mid m\); parity and residues modulo \(3\) exclude \(p=2,3\). An elementary residue bound makes each such forced power at least \(n\), so if \(q\) were composite then either a repeated least prime factor would force a divisor at least \(n^2\), or two distinct prime factors would force a coprime product at least \(n^2\), contradicting \(m=n^2-2\); the boundary case \(n=3\) is computed directly.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S_r=\sum_{k=0}^r k!,\qquad A_r=\frac{(r+2)S_r}{2}\quad(r\geq 0).
\]
The numbers \(A_r\) are integers. Indeed, if \(r\) is even then \(r+2\) is even. If \(r\) is odd, then \(r\geq1\), and \(S_r\) is even: the first two terms are \(0!+1!=2\), while every \(k!\) with \(k\geq2\) is even. Thus in all cases
\[
2A_r=(r+2)S_r. \tag{1}
\]
These \(A_r\) are the terms of the auxiliary sequence A051403 used in the formula for A363102.

We first recall how the formula for the denominator follows from the continued fraction. Starting at the innermost end, put \(T_n=-2\), and for \(k=n-1,n-2,\ldots,2\), put
\[
T_k=k-\frac{k+1}{T_{k+1}}.
\]
If \(T_k=P_k/Q_k\) is kept as an unreduced fraction, then one may take
\[
P_n=-2,\quad Q_n=1,
\]
and
\[
P_k=kP_{k+1}-(k+1)Q_{k+1},\qquad Q_k=P_{k+1}. \tag{2}
\]
Consequently the full continued fraction is \(1/T_2=Q_2/P_2\). Applying (2) successively, and using \(S_{r+1}=S_r+(r+1)!\), gives
\[
P_2=-(n^2-2),
\qquad
Q_2=-\bigl(2A_{n-3}+nA_{n-4}\bigr).
\]
This is the standard continuant evaluation of the displayed finite continued fraction; it can also be checked directly by backward induction in (2), with (1) used to clear the factors \(2\). Hence, after reducing the fraction, its positive denominator is
\[
a(n)=\frac{n^2-2}{\gcd(n^2-2,D_n)},
\qquad
D_n:=2A_{n-3}+nA_{n-4}. \tag{3}
\]
For \(n=3\), the convention in (3) gives \(A_0=1\) for both truncated indices, exactly as a direct evaluation of \(1/(2-3/(-2))\) does.

We shall prove that the integer in (3) is either \(1\) or prime.

For the main argument assume first that \(n\geq4\), and abbreviate
\[
m=n^2-2,\qquad D=D_n,
\qquad g=\gcd(m,D),\qquad q=\frac m g=a(n).
\]
Both \(m\) and \(D\) are positive. In particular, \(q\) is positive and \(q\mid m\).

The central identity is
\[
2D=2(n-1)(n-3)!+mS_{n-4}. \tag{4}
\]
To prove it, use (1):
\[
\begin{aligned}
2D
 &=4A_{n-3}+2nA_{n-4}\\
 &=2(n-1)S_{n-3}+n(n-2)S_{n-4}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(S_{n-3}=S_{n-4}+(n-3)!\), this becomes
\[
2(n-1)(n-3)!+ igl(2(n-1)+n(n-2)\bigr)S_{n-4},
\]
and the coefficient in parentheses is \(n^2-2=m\), proving (4).

We need several elementary facts about prime divisors of \(m\).

First, \(3\nmid m\). Indeed, every square modulo \(3\) is \(0\) or \(1\), so \(n^2-2\) is congruent to \(1\) or \(2\), never \(0\), modulo \(3\).

Second, \(4\nmid m\), because every square modulo \(4\) is \(0\) or \(1\), whereas adding \(2\) to a multiple of \(4\) cannot give either residue.

We next show that \(q\) is odd. If \(n\) is odd, then \(m=n^2-2\) is odd, and so is every divisor \(q\) of \(m\). If \(n\) is even, then \(m\) is even but not divisible by \(4\), so its \(2\)-adic valuation is exactly \(1\). On the other hand,
\[
D=2A_{n-3}+nA_{n-4}
\]
is even, because both summands are even. Thus the gcd \(g=\gcd(m,D)\) contains the entire factor \(2\) occurring in \(m\), and \(q=m/g\) is again odd. Therefore
\[
2\nmid q. \tag{5}
\]

Now let \(p\) be an odd prime divisor of \(m\). We claim that
\[
p\nmid n-2\quad\hbox{and}\quad p\nmid n-1. \tag{6}
\]
If \(p\mid n-2\), then \(n\equiv2\pmod p\), so from \(p\mid n^2-2\) we obtain \(p\mid 2\); since \(p\) is prime this would force \(p=2\), contrary to its being odd. If \(p\mid n-1\), then \(n\equiv1\pmod p\), and \(p\mid n^2-2\) would imply \(p\mid1\), which is impossible. This proves (6).

Write the Euclidean division of \(n-3\) by \(p\) as
\[
n-3=pf+r,
\qquad
f=\left\lfloor\frac{n-3}{p}\right\rfloor,
\qquad 0\leq r<p.
\]
The last two possible values of \(r\) cannot occur. If \(r=p-1\), then
\[
n-2=p(f+1),
\]
contradicting \(p\nmid n-2\). If \(r=p-2\), then
\[
n-1=p(f+1),
\]
contradicting \(p\nmid n-1\). Thus \(r\leq p-3\), and hence
\[
n=pf+r+3\leq p(f+1). \tag{7}
\]

We shall also use two elementary growth estimates. For \(p\geq2\) and \(f\geq0\),
\[
f+1\leq p^f. \tag{8}
\]
This follows by induction on \(f\). It is equality for \(f=0\). If it holds for \(f\), then
\[
f+2\leq2(f+1)\leq p(f+1)\leq p^{f+1}.
\]
For \(p\geq4\), we similarly have
\[
(f+1)^2\leq p^f. \tag{9}
\]
Again the assertion is clear for \(f=0\). For the induction step,
\[
(f+2)^2\leq4(f+1)^2\leq p(f+1)^2\leq p^{f+1};
\]
the first inequality follows from \(f+2\leq2(f+1)\).

We now prove the key prime-power footprint lemma.

**Footprint lemma.** Let \(p\) be an odd prime dividing \(m=n^2-2\), let \(j\geq1\), and suppose that \(p^j\mid q\). Put
\[
f=\left\lfloor\frac{n-3}{p}\right\rfloor.
\]
Then
\[
p^{f+j}\mid m. \tag{10}
\]

To prove this, write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\), and set
\[
V=v_p(m),\quad W=v_p(D),\quad B=v_p((n-3)!).
\]
Legendre’s formula for the exponent of a prime in a factorial says
\[
v_p((n-3)!)=
\left\lfloor\frac{n-3}{p}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{n-3}{p^2}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac{n-3}{p^3}\right\rfloor+
\cdots.
\]
All terms are nonnegative, so
\[
B\geq f. \tag{11}
\]

Let \(K=\min(B,V)\). Then \(p^K\) divides both \((n-3)!\) and \(m\). By identity (4), it follows that \(p^K\mid2D\). Since \(p\) is odd, \(p^K\) is coprime to \(2\), and consequently \(p^K\mid D\). Thus
\[
W\geq\min(B,V). \tag{12}
\]

Because \(g=\gcd(m,D)\),
\[
v_p(g)=\min(V,W).
\]
Also \(m=gq\), and therefore
\[
V=\min(V,W)+v_p(q). \tag{13}
\]
Our assumption \(p^j\mid q\) gives \(v_p(q)\geq j\). From (12),
\[
\min(V,W)\geq\min(B,V).
\]
If \(V<B\), equations (12) and (13) would imply
\[
V\geq V+j,
\]
which is impossible because \(j\geq1\). Hence \(V\geq B\), and then (12) and (13) give
\[
V\geq B+j\geq f+j
\]
by (11). This is exactly (10), proving the footprint lemma.

We now finish the proof for \(n\geq4\). Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(q\neq1\) and that \(q\) is not prime. Since \(q>0\), we have \(q\geq2\). Let \(p\) be the least prime divisor of \(q\). Then \(p\mid m\). By (5), \(p\neq2\), and by the earlier congruence argument, \(p\neq3\). Therefore
\[
p\geq5. \tag{14}
\]
Since \(q\) is not prime, it is not equal to its least prime divisor \(p\). Thus \(q/p\geq2\). Let \(p_2\) be the least prime divisor of \(q/p\). Then \(p_2\) is prime, \(p_2\mid q\), and by the minimality of \(p\),
\[
p\leq p_2.
\]
Also \(p_2\neq2\), because \(q\) is odd. There are two cases.

**Case 1: \(p_2=p\).** In this case \(p\mid q/p\), so \(p^2\mid q\). Apply the footprint lemma with \(j=2\). If
\[
f=\left\lfloor\frac{n-3}{p}\right\rfloor,
\]
then
\[
p^{f+2}\mid m. \tag{15}
\]
On the other hand, (7) gives \(n\leq p(f+1)\), and (9), applicable because \(p\geq5\), gives \((f+1)^2\leq p^f\). Therefore
\[
n^2\leq p^2(f+1)^2\leq p^{f+2}. \tag{16}
\]
Since the positive integer \(p^{f+2}\) divides the positive integer \(m\), (15) also gives
\[
p^{f+2}\leq m=n^2-2. \tag{17}
\]
Combining (16) and (17) yields \(n^2\leq n^2-2\), a contradiction.

**Case 2: \(p<p_2\).** Put
\[
f_1=\left\lfloor\frac{n-3}{p}\right\rfloor,
\qquad
f_2=\left\lfloor\frac{n-3}{p_2}\right\rfloor.
\]
Applying the footprint lemma with \(j=1\) first to \(p\) and then to \(p_2\) gives
\[
p^{f_1+1}\mid m,
\qquad
p_2^{f_2+1}\mid m. \tag{18}
\]
For either of these primes, (7) and (8) imply
\[
n\leq (f_i+1)p_i\leq p_i^{f_i}p_i=p_i^{f_i+1}. \tag{19}
\]
Since \(p\) and \(p_2\) are distinct primes, the two prime powers in (18) are coprime. Their product therefore divides \(m\):
\[
p^{f_1+1}p_2^{f_2+1}\mid m. \tag{20}
\]
By (19), this product is at least \(n^2\), while by (20), being a positive divisor of \(m\), it is at most \(m=n^2-2\). Once again we obtain the impossible inequality
\[
n^2\leq n^2-2.
\]

Both cases are impossible. Consequently, for every \(n\geq4\), \(q=a(n)\) must be either \(1\) or prime.

It remains only to handle \(n=3\). Here \(A_0=1\), so formula (3) gives
\[
m=3^2-2=7,
\qquad
D=2A_0+3A_0=5,
\]
and hence
\[
a(3)=\frac7{\gcd(7,5)}=7,
\]
which is prime.

Thus for every integer \(n\geq3\), the denominator of the stated continued fraction is either \(1\) or a prime.
